prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cells, tissues, organs and body systems
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach a cell as a structural unit, a tissue as an organised group of cells, an organ as a structure containing tissues, and a body system as cooperating organs. This supplies the organisational scale needed for the four tissue categories and their locations.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach the cell membrane as the cell boundary, cytoplasm as the material within it outside the nucleus, and the nucleus as the genetic-control compartment. Learners must distinguish whole cells, internal parts, multiple nuclei and the neuron's signalling route.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Covering, lining, cavities and compartments
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach covering as lying over a surface, lining as covering an internal surface, and a cavity as an internal space. Explain a compartment as a separated body region so that epithelial barrier functions have a concrete meaning.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell shapes, layers and tissue surfaces
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach flattened, cube-like, tall slender, cylindrical and spindle-shaped forms, and contrast one cell layer with several layers. Identify the free surface, the lower or basal region, and central versus peripheral positions before interpreting diagrams.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Extracellular material, intercellular space and fibres
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach extracellular as outside cells, intercellular as between cells, matrix as surrounding extracellular material, and fibres as thread-like extracellular components. Explain a cell process as an extension of a cell; this distinguishes epithelial cementing material, basement membrane, connective matrix and bone-cell processes.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Diffusion across a thin barrier
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient and explain that a shorter path can facilitate exchange. This makes the single thin squamous layer's association with diffusion understandable.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Absorption, secretion, glands and ducts
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach absorption as taking substances across a surface, secretion as release of a substance from a cell, a gland as a secretory structure, and a duct as a passage carrying glandular output. Explain multicellular as composed of multiple cells.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cilia, microvilli and mucus
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach cilia as hair-like surface projections whose coordinated beating can move material, microvilli as small projections increasing surface area, and mucus as a slippery secretion. These definitions prevent confusion between surface-area enhancement and directed surface transport.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Blood vessels, capillaries and lung air sacs
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach blood vessels as blood-carrying passages, capillaries as small exchange vessels, and lung air sacs as gas-exchange spaces. These are the concrete sites needed to learn the simple squamous row.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Kidney tubules, proximal convoluted tubules and Bowman's capsule
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach Bowman's capsule as the cup-like beginning of a kidney filtration unit and kidney tubules as passages involved in processing the filtrate, with the proximal convoluted tubule as an early coiled segment. Keep capsule lining and tubular lining distinct when learning the epithelial examples.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Digestive and respiratory passages, urethra and named glands
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Locate the digestive passage, upper respiratory passage, male urethra, mammary glands, sweat glands and salivary glands at a simple anatomical level. Explain that lobar ducts are ducts associated with gland lobes, so the table's location labels can be understood rather than memorised as unfamiliar words.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Cell division, metabolism, shedding and abrasion
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach cell division as production of new cells, metabolism as cellular chemical activity, shedding as loss of surface cells, and abrasion as surface wear. These ideas explain renewal of the protective stratified squamous lining.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Muscle contraction, muscle fibres and striations
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach contraction as force generation that can produce shortening or tension, muscle fibre as the elongated muscle-cell unit in this context, and striations as visible transverse bands. This supplies the vocabulary for appearance and movement without requiring molecular contraction mechanisms.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Voluntary and involuntary control
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach voluntary control as conscious control of an action and involuntary activity as activity that does not ordinarily require a conscious command. Use these meanings before comparing the muscle rows.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Skeleton, heart circulation and smooth-muscle target structures
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Locate the skeleton and heart, explain that the heart pumps blood, identify the uterus and the pupil as the eye's opening, and define blood pressure as pressure exerted by blood within vessels. Define peristalsis as a coordinated travelling contraction so the muscle functions can be interpreted.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Blood components and their broad roles
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Distinguish white blood cells associated with defence, red blood cells associated with oxygen transport, and platelets associated with clotting at damaged vessels. Treat these as explanatory foundations, not as functions printed beside the supplied blood-cell labels.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Connective-tissue cell names and matrix vocabulary
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach osteocyte as a bone cell, chondrocyte as a cartilage cell, and adipocyte as a fat-storage cell. Introduce collagen and reticular fibres as extracellular network components and fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell and plasma cell as distinct cell names, avoiding the assumption that fibre labels name cells.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Phagocytosis, inflammation and antibodies as optional vocabulary support
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: If immune terms are used to explain the labelled cells, first teach phagocytosis as engulfment of material, inflammation as a response to injury or infection, and antibodies as proteins involved in specific defence; plasma cells are antibody-secreting cells derived from B lymphocytes. These are outside clarifications, not additional functions asserted by the supplied areolar or blood-cell diagrams.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Lipids, fat storage and nuclear position
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach fat as a lipid stored within cells and usable as an energy reserve. Explain that a large intracellular droplet can occupy much of the cell interior, preparing learners to interpret the adipocyte's marginal nucleus.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Stimulus and a nerve impulse
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach a stimulus as a detectable change and a nerve impulse as an electrical signal travelling along a neuron's membrane. Explain that ions are charged particles whose movement across membranes contributes to electrical signalling; detailed action-potential phases are unnecessary here.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Separate neurons, synaptic gaps and neurotransmitter receptors
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach that communicating neurons remain separate cells, that a synapse is a specialised communication junction, and that neurotransmitters are chemical messengers acting on receiving-membrane receptors. This makes the transition from an electrical signal along an axon to communication with another cell understandable.

prerequisites_to_teach.name: Reading labels, arrows and separate diagram panels
prerequisites_to_teach.why_needed: Teach pointer lines as identifiers and directional arrows as indicators of movement or sequence, while recognising that adjacent panels may simply compare examples. This prevents treating the epithelial blocks or connective-tissue panels as developmental stages.

exam_focus.why: Book-based target: Four-way tissue classification and function matching provide the framework for direct questions and odd-one-out items.
Book-based target: Tight packing, minimal intercellular spaces and an extracellular basement membrane are distinctive structural statements; distinguish basement membrane from cell membrane.
Book-based target: Secretory specialisation and inward folding into a multicellular gland connect epithelial structure with gland formation.
Book-based target: Recognising flattened, cuboidal, stratified and ciliated columnar forms supports diagram questions; the blocks are comparisons, not sequential stages.
Book-based target: Match simple squamous structure and diffusion with capillaries, vessel lining, lung air sacs and Bowman's capsule.
Book-based target: Kidney tubules, glandular ducts, absorption, secretion and proximal-convoluted-tubule microvilli form a high-value matching set.
Book-based target: Tall single-layer cells, cilia, mucus secretion and directed movement are useful for structure–function questions; retain the table's stated locations.
Book-based target: Mouth and vagina, protective layers, active lower cells and flattened shedding surface cells support location and statement-combination questions.
Book-based target: Gland-associated locations and protection of ducts distinguish stratified cuboidal from simple cuboidal tissue.
Book-based target: Male urethra and lobar salivary ducts are distinctive locations; columnar surface cells need not imply identical lower layers.
Book-based target: The three muscle types must be compared simultaneously across location, function, appearance and control.
Book-based target: Voluntary, striated, parallel fibres with multiple eccentric nuclei distinguish skeletal muscle; retain heat and posture alongside movement.
Book-based target: Cardiac muscle is the key exception to associating striations with voluntary control; branching and a central nucleus aid identification.
Book-based target: Smooth muscle combines involuntary control, absent striations and spindle-shaped cells; peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size and hair erection are matching targets.
Book-based target: Blood, bone, cartilage, areolar tissue and adipose tissue belong within the connective-tissue examples despite their different appearances.
Book-based target: Recognise the five named white blood corpuscles and visible nuclear distinctions; do not require the uncertain neutrophil parenthetical text.
Book-based target: Platelet fragments and the separately drawn red blood corpuscle should not be misclassified as one of the named white blood cells.
Book-based target: Haversian canal versus canaliculus is a precise structure–contents distinction: vessels and nerve fibres versus an osteocyte process.
Book-based target: Chondrocyte identifies a cartilage cell, while hyaline matrix identifies its extracellular surroundings.
Book-based target: Distinguish collagen and reticular fibres from fibroblast, macrophage, mast cell and plasma cell; this supports diagram labelling and odd-one-out questions.
Book-based target: Large fat droplets, marginal nuclei and the adipocyte label are the defining features shown for adipose tissue.
Book-based target: Identify dendrites, cell body, nucleus, axon and axon tips across successive neurons, without treating the nucleus as part of the signal route.

Book-based target: This directly answers the supplied question and tests direction along the axon and contacts at synapses; the additional neurotransmitter mechanism must remain labelled as outside explanation.
